summary: A humorous first-person account of the author's first marathon, from impulsively registering after a neighbor's encouragement through months of training to the race itself, described mile by mile. The author goes from cheerful optimism to exhaustion, delirium and a limping finish. The author concludes that the main thing conquered was their own better judgment and jokes that readers should click "Cancel" instead of "Register."
one_line: A comic mile-by-mile recounting of the author's first marathon, prompted by neighbor Bob McGee, ending in a finish and doubts about the whole idea.
key_facts: The author's marathon distance was 26.2 miles; the author nicknames the experience "The Longest Slog."
The note opens by referring to September 5, 2023, but the forecast and race are described as October 7th, and the post is dated October 12, 2023.
Neighbor Bob "Buns of Steel" McGee suggested the marathon, saying "You know what you need? A marathon! It's life-changing."
Bob McGee is described as an obscenely fit person who flips tractor tires for fun.
The author followed a training regimen from internet former high school track coaches, ran in rain and heat, and was motivated by post-run pizza slices; weight was lost and muscles were found.
The October 7th forecast predicted ideal running conditions, but the author felt nervous at the starting line among thousands of runners.
In miles 1-6 the author felt optimistic, high-fived a toddler and thought "I am a gazelle."
By mile ten, water stations felt like oases, and the running app's notifications began to feel like taunts.
Around mile 14 the author saw runners with cramps and reflected on the Greek soldier who ran from Marathon to Athens and died.
During miles 22-24 the author's run became a "zombie shuffle" and was overtaken by a man the author believed was at least 85.
At mile 25 a lady with a megaphone shouting "You can do it!" became the author's momentary hero.
The author finished with arms raised, took a participation medal, and felt they had only conquered their own better judgment.
Bob was at the finish line and asked "Life-changing, right?"
